GENETICS / MOLECULAR__Haematological Mal:
The JAK2 V617F, CALR and MPL mutations are somatic driver mutations that constitutively activate the JAK-STAT signalling pathway, driving clonal overproduction of blood cells. They are the molecular cornerstone for diagnosing BCR-ABL1–negative myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) — polycythaemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythaemia (ET) and primary myelofibrosis (PMF). Detecting one on peripheral blood establishes clonality and, alongside the blood count and marrow, satisfies WHO diagnostic criteria.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Order molecular testing when the blood count suggests an MPN: a persistently raised haematocrit/haemoglobin (query PV), an unexplained sustained thrombocytosis ≥ 450 × 10&sup9;/L (query ET), or leucoerythroblastic film with tear-drop cells and splenomegaly (query PMF). The biological principle is constitutive JAK-STAT activation: JAK2 is a tyrosine kinase coupled to the erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and G-CSF receptors. The V617F substitution in the auto-inhibitory JH2 pseudokinase domain locks JAK2 “on”, so cells proliferate independently of growth-factor stimulation — hence the low/suppressed erythropoietin in PV.

JAK2 V617F — a single G→T point mutation (valine→phenylalanine at codon 617).
CALR (calreticulin) and MPL (thrombopoietin receptor) mutations activate the same pathway in JAK2-negative ET/PMF.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Testing is done on a simple peripheral blood EDTA sample — no bone marrow is required to find the mutation (though marrow may still be needed for WHO staging and to grade fibrosis). A tiered laboratory algorithm is used:

First line: allele-specific real-time PCR for JAK2 V617F (quantitative, reports an allele burden %). Highly sensitive, cheap, rapid.
If PV suspected but V617F-negative: sequence JAK2 exon 12 (accounts for most remaining PV).
If ET/PMF suspected but V617F-negative: test CALR exon 9 then MPL exon 10 mutations.

Modern labs increasingly use a targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) myeloid panel that covers all three genes simultaneously.

3INTERPRETATION

Mutation prevalence differs sharply by disease, so the result meaningfully narrows the diagnosis:

JAK2 V617F positive + raised Hct + low EPO→Polycythaemia vera (V617F present in ~95% of PV)
JAK2 V617F positive + isolated thrombocytosis→Essential thrombocythaemia (V617F in ~50–60% of ET)
JAK2-negative ET/PMF, CALR mutated→CALR-mutant ET or PMF (~20–25%); better prognosis in PMF
JAK2- and CALR-negative ET/PMF, MPL mutated→MPL-mutant ET/PMF (~3–5%)
All three negative (“triple-negative”)→MPN not excluded — ~10–15% of ET/PMF; needs marrow & clinical correlation
🧪JAK2 V617F
~95% PV; ~50–60% ET & PMF; the key first-line test
🧬CALR
JAK2-negative ET/PMF; higher platelets, lower thrombosis risk
🔬MPL
Small subset of JAK2/CALR-negative ET/PMF

Presence of a driver mutation is a major WHO diagnostic criterion for each MPN, confirming clonality and separating a true neoplasm from a reactive (secondary) cause such as hypoxia, dehydration, iron deficiency, inflammation or malignancy.

4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
A negative test does not exclude an MPN — triple-negative disease exists, and secondary erythrocytosis/thrombocytosis must still be worked up.
A positive JAK2 does not name the disease by itself — the same mutation occurs across PV, ET and PMF, so it must be integrated with the full blood count, EPO level and marrow morphology.
Low allele burden can occasionally be found in older people without overt MPN (clonal haematopoiesis); interpret in clinical context.
🚩 MPNs carry a high arterial and venous thrombosis risk, which is often the presenting event and a leading cause of death in PV and ET. Test for JAK2 V617F in any unexplained splanchnic-vein thrombosis — Budd-Chiari syndrome, portal or mesenteric vein thrombosis — because an MPN may be present even with a near-normal blood count (masked by portal hypertension and haemodilution).
🎓 A raised haematocrit with a low or normal erythropoietin points to primary (clonal) polycythaemia — check JAK2 V617F; a high EPO points to a secondary cause (hypoxia, high-altitude, EPO-secreting tumour). In JAK2-negative ET/PMF, CALR mutation carries a more favourable prognosis and lower thrombotic risk than JAK2-mutant disease.

The BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (Philadelphia chromosome) is the defining molecular lesion of chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML). It arises from a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22, producing a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives unregulated myeloid proliferation. Detecting it confirms the diagnosis, and quantifying its transcript level tracks how well a patient is responding to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Requested to confirm CML in a patient with a raised white cell count, marked neutrophilia with a left shift (myelocytes, metamyelocytes), basophilia, and often splenomegaly. It is also sought in a subset of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (Ph-positive ALL).

The t(9;22)(q34;q11) translocation fuses the BCR gene on chromosome 22 to the ABL1 gene on chromosome 9.
The shortened chromosome 22 is the Philadelphia chromosome.
The resulting BCR-ABL1 protein is a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that switches on proliferation and blocks apoptosis independent of normal growth signals.
In CML the fusion typically produces a p210 protein; Ph-positive ALL more often produces a smaller p190.
🧬FISH
Detects the BCR-ABL1 fusion signal in interphase cells; rapid and sensitive at diagnosis
🔬Karyotype
Cytogenetics shows the Philadelphia chromosome and any additional clonal changes
🧪RT-qPCR
Quantifies BCR-ABL1 transcript level; the mainstay for monitoring on treatment
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

At diagnosis, a peripheral blood sample (and often a bone marrow aspirate for karyotyping) is analysed. Cytogenetics and FISH establish the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, while quantitative RT-PCR establishes the baseline transcript burden.

Blood is collected in EDTA; RNA is extracted and reverse-transcribed to cDNA.
BCR-ABL1 transcripts are amplified and quantified against a control gene, then reported on the International Scale (IS) as a percentage (BCR-ABL1IS%).
On treatment, monitoring is repeated at regular intervals (commonly every 3 months) to chart the log reduction from the standardised baseline.
3INTERPRETATION

Diagnosis is a yes/no: the presence of BCR-ABL1 confirms CML. Response to a tyrosine kinase inhibitor is graded by how far the transcript level falls on the International Scale.

BCR-ABL1 detected (FISH / karyotype / PCR)→Confirms chronic myeloid leukaemia
BCR-ABL1IS ≤ 10% at 3 months→Early molecular response – on track
BCR-ABL1IS ≤ 1%→Equivalent to complete cytogenetic response
BCR-ABL1IS ≤ 0.1% (3-log reduction)→Major molecular response (MMR / MR3)
BCR-ABL1IS ≤ 0.01% (MR4) or undetectable (MR4.5)→Deep molecular response – may allow trial of treatment-free remission
4PITFALLS & SAFETY
Results must be reported on the International Scale so that values are comparable between laboratories and over time.
A single low-level rise can reflect assay variation; a confirmed, sustained rise (typically ≥ 5-fold with loss of MMR) is what signals treatment failure.
Loss of response should prompt an assessment of adherence and testing for kinase domain mutations.
🚩 Rising BCR-ABL1 transcripts on therapy indicate relapse or acquired resistance. Send a kinase domain mutation analysis: the T315I mutation confers resistance to imatinib and most second-generation inhibitors, and mandates a switch of therapy (e.g. ponatinib).
🎓 Imatinib is the classic targeted therapy for CML – it is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor that binds the ATP pocket of the BCR-ABL1 protein and shuts off its kinase activity. Achieving a major molecular response (BCR-ABL1IS ≤ 0.1%) is the key monitoring milestone.

The PML-RARα fusion gene, produced by the balanced translocation t(15;17)(q24;q21), defines acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML / APL / AML-M3). Detecting it is a molecular emergency: the fusion oncoprotein blocks myeloid maturation at the promyelocyte stage, and the abnormal promyelocytes release procoagulant granules that drive severe disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Rapid confirmation by PCR/FISH plus immediate ATRA therapy transforms the most fatal early AML into the best-prognosis subtype.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE — why we hunt for the fusion

Any patient with a suspected acute leukaemia — pancytopenia, blasts on film, or unexplained bleeding/bruising — must be screened for APML, because it is the one AML subtype where a delay of hours costs lives. The translocation fuses the PML gene on chromosome 15 to the retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARα) gene on chromosome 17.

The PML-RARα oncoprotein binds retinoic-acid response elements and recruits co-repressors, arresting differentiation at the promyelocyte stage.
Abnormal promyelocytes are packed with granules rich in tissue factor and annexin II, triggering catastrophic DIC and hyperfibrinolysis.
Pharmacological doses of retinoic acid (ATRA) overcome the block, so the same lesion that causes the disease is also its therapeutic target.
2HOW IT IS DETECTED — the diagnostic protocol

Diagnosis is confirmed on bone marrow (or peripheral blood) using complementary techniques with different turnaround times:

🧪RT-PCR
Detects the PML-RARα transcript; also gives a baseline for monitoring measurable residual disease (MRD).
🔬FISH
Dual-colour probes show fusion signal within hours — rapid confirmation of t(15;17).
🧬Karyotype
Metaphase cytogenetics confirms t(15;17)(q24;q21) but is slower (days).
🩸Blood film
Hypergranular promyelocytes, bundles of Auer rods (faggot cells) — the immediate bedside clue.

Immunophenotype is characteristic: CD33+, CD13+, MPO strongly positive, HLA-DR negative, CD34 usually negative.

3INTERPRETATION — coagulation values & morphology

The coagulopathy is monitored alongside the molecular result:

Faggot cells / multiple Auer rods on film→Presumptive APML — treat as emergency before genetics return
Fibrinogen < 1.5 g/L (often < 1.0)→Active DIC — replace with cryoprecipitate, aim fibrinogen ≥ 1.5 g/L
Platelets < 30–50 ×10&sup9;/L→Transfuse platelets to keep ≥ 30–50 ×10&sup9;/L while coagulopathic
Rising D-dimer, prolonged PT/APTT, schistocytes→Consumptive coagulopathy with hyperfibrinolysis confirmed
PML-RARα positive by PCR/FISH→Diagnosis confirmed — continue ATRA + arsenic trioxide (ATO)
PML-RARα negative→Not classic APML — reassess; ATRA-resistant variants (e.g. ZBTB16-RARα) exist
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & TREATMENT PRINCIPLE
Treat on suspicion: ATRA is started before molecular confirmation because the coagulopathy kills within hours; it is safe to stop if APML is excluded.
Avoid the wrong reflex: aggressive cytotoxic chemotherapy alone can worsen tumour lysis and bleeding — ATRA + arsenic trioxide is the differentiating backbone in low/intermediate-risk disease.
Cryptic fusions: a small minority have submicroscopic insertions that karyotype misses — hence PCR/FISH are essential, not optional.
Monitor MRD: serial RT-PCR after consolidation detects molecular relapse before clinical relapse.
🚩 APML with DIC is a haematological emergency. Start ATRA immediately on clinical or morphological suspicion — do NOT wait for cytogenetic confirmation. Support coagulation aggressively (cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen, platelets, FFP). Beware differentiation syndrome (ATRA/ATO syndrome): fever, dyspnoea, pulmonary infiltrates, weight gain, oedema, hypotension — treat urgently with high-dose dexamethasone and consider pausing the differentiating agent.
🎓 APML is the best-prognosis AML and the classic "treat-before-you-confirm" leukaemia: the PML-RARα block is ATRA-responsive, so all-trans retinoic acid plus arsenic trioxide can cure the majority — chemotherapy-free in low-risk disease. Remember it as the malignancy where the targeted therapy came before we fully understood the target.

Lymphoma translocations are recurrent chromosomal rearrangements that juxtapose a cellular oncogene to the powerful immunoglobulin heavy-chain (IGH) enhancer on chromosome 14q32, driving constitutive over-expression of the partner gene. Three are classically examined: t(14;18) in follicular lymphoma, t(8;14) in Burkitt lymphoma, and t(11;14) in mantle cell lymphoma. Detecting them by FISH or PCR confirms the diagnosis, refines WHO classification, and can carry prognostic weight.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

B lymphocytes physically break and rejoin their IGH locus during normal V(D)J recombination and class-switching. An aberrant recombination event can splice a proto-oncogene next to the IGH enhancer, which is highly active in B cells, so the oncogene is transcribed at pathologically high levels. This is the shared mechanism behind these lymphomas.

Used when a mature B-cell lymphoma is suspected on morphology/immunophenotype and a defining genetic lesion is needed to confirm subtype.
Also resolves difficult cases (e.g. distinguishing mantle cell from other small B-cell lymphomas) where immunohistochemistry is equivocal.
2HOW IT IS DETECTED

Tissue is obtained by excisional lymph node biopsy (preferred over core/needle for architecture). Two main techniques are applied to the sample:

FISH — fluorescent probes flanking the breakpoint; a "break-apart" or "dual-fusion" signal pattern confirms the rearrangement. Works on paraffin-embedded tissue and detects most breakpoints.
PCR — amplifies the fusion junction (e.g. BCL2–IGH); highly sensitive but only detects breakpoints within the primed region, so a negative PCR does not exclude the translocation.
Immunohistochemistry gives a surrogate readout of the over-expressed protein (BCL2, cyclin D1) and Ki-67 quantifies the proliferation fraction.
3INTERPRETATION

Each translocation maps to a specific over-expressed protein and lymphoma subtype:

t(14;18) — BCL2 to IGH→Follicular lymphoma; BCL2 blocks apoptosis (anti-apoptotic), cells accumulate
t(8;14) — MYC to IGH→Burkitt lymphoma; MYC drives proliferation, "starry-sky" histology, Ki-67 ≥ 95%
t(11;14) — CCND1 to IGH→Mantle cell lymphoma; cyclin D1 over-expression pushes G1→S cell-cycle entry
🧬BCL2
Anti-apoptotic; follicular lymphoma; indolent
⚡MYC
Pro-proliferation; Burkitt; highly aggressive
🔁Cyclin D1
Cell-cycle driver; mantle cell; SOX11 positive
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
A translocation alone is not proof of malignancy — low-level BCL2–IGH can be found in reactive lymphoid tissue and healthy blood; interpret alongside morphology and clonality.
Negative PCR does not exclude disease (breakpoint outside amplified region); FISH is more robust for confirming a rearrangement.
"Double-hit" lymphomas carry MYC plus BCL2 (or BCL6) rearrangements and behave far more aggressively than follicular lymphoma — always test for a second hit.
🚩 Burkitt lymphoma has one of the fastest doubling times of any human tumour. Starting chemotherapy causes massive cell death and tumour lysis syndrome — hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and acute kidney injury. Give prophylactic IV fluids and rasburicase and monitor closely; TLS can be fatal.
🎓 Memory hook: t(14;18) = Follicular (BCL2), t(8;14) = Burkitt (MYC), t(11;14) = Mantle cell (cyclin D1). Chromosome 14 (IGH) is the constant partner in all three.

A thrombophilia panel is a battery of laboratory tests that screens for inherited and acquired hypercoagulable states in patients with venous thromboembolism (VTE). It identifies why blood clots too readily — either a gain-of-function mutation making clotting factors resistant to shutdown, or a deficiency of the body's own natural anticoagulants — and helps stratify recurrence risk. Crucially, the panel is only useful when the right patient is tested at the right time: tested carelessly during acute clot or on anticoagulation, it produces dangerously misleading results.

1INDICATION — who and why

Thrombosis reflects Virchow's triad: hypercoagulability, stasis and endothelial injury. The panel probes the hypercoagulable limb — either too much procoagulant activity (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A) or too little natural anticoagulant (protein C, protein S, antithrombin), plus the acquired antiphospholipid syndrome. Testing is selective, not routine, because most results do not change management.

Test if: unprovoked VTE in a young patient (<45), recurrent VTE, thrombosis at an unusual site (cerebral, splanchnic, portal vein), strong family history, or recurrent pregnancy loss (for antiphospholipid).
Generally do NOT test if: a single provoked VTE (surgery, long-haul flight, plaster cast) — a clear precipitant already explains the clot and heritable results rarely alter treatment duration.
2THE COMPONENTS — what is measured
🧬Factor V Leiden
Point mutation makes factor V resistant to inactivation by activated protein C (APC resistance). Commonest inherited thrombophilia.
🧬Prothrombin G20210A
Gene mutation raising prothrombin (factor II) levels. Second commonest; genetic PCR test, unaffected by acute clot.
🛡️Protein C
Vitamin-K-dependent natural anticoagulant; deficiency → unopposed clotting. Falsely low on warfarin / in acute clot.
🛡️Protein S
Cofactor for protein C; also vitamin-K-dependent. Lowered by warfarin, pregnancy and oestrogen.
🛡️Antithrombin
Chief inhibitor of thrombin and factor Xa; heparin's target. Consumed in acute clot and lowered by heparin.
🌙Antiphospholipid
Acquired: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-β₂-glycoprotein-I antibodies. Needs confirmation at 12 weeks.
3HOW IT IS PERFORMED — timing is everything

The panel mixes genetic PCR tests (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A — stable, testable any time) with functional / activity assays (protein C, protein S, antithrombin) and immunoassays / clotting tests (antiphospholipid). The functional assays are exquisitely sensitive to the clinical context:

Not during acute thrombosis: natural anticoagulants are consumed as the clot forms, giving falsely low levels.
Not on anticoagulation: warfarin lowers protein C & S; heparin lowers antithrombin. Ideally test off-anticoagulant, or defer — commonly ≥2 weeks after stopping warfarin and once the acute event has resolved.
Antiphospholipid: a positive result must be repeated ≥12 weeks apart to confirm persistence before the syndrome is diagnosed.
4INTERPRETATION — results to actions
Positive Factor V Leiden PCR (heterozygous)→APC resistance confirmed; ~3–8× VTE risk — commonest inherited thrombophilia
Homozygous Factor V Leiden→Markedly higher risk than heterozygous; stronger consideration of extended anticoagulation
Low protein C, protein S or antithrombin activity→Suggests deficiency — but confirm timing (not acute, off anticoagulant) and repeat before labelling
Antithrombin deficiency→Most thrombogenic inherited defect; may cause apparent heparin resistance
Lupus anticoagulant / anticardiolipin / anti-β₂GPI positive, repeated at 12 weeks→Antiphospholipid syndrome — warfarin (not DOAC) is preferred for anticoagulation
Prolonged APTT not correcting on 50:50 mix→Points to lupus anticoagulant (an in-vitro inhibitor), not a factor deficiency
🚩 Do NOT measure protein C, protein S or antithrombin during an acute clot or while on warfarin/heparin — the results are falsely altered and a spurious “deficiency” can trigger wrong lifelong labelling and family testing. Defer functional assays until the acute event has settled and anticoagulation is stopped or switched appropriately. A positive antiphospholipid antibody must always be repeated ≥12 weeks later before the syndrome is diagnosed.
🎓 Factor V Leiden is the commonest inherited thrombophilia in Caucasians and causes activated protein C (APC) resistance — the classic exam link. Prothrombin G20210A is second. Because both are DNA/PCR tests, they are the only panel components reliably valid during acute clot and on anticoagulation.

The G6PD assay quantifies red-cell glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity to diagnose G6PD deficiency — the commonest human enzymopathy and an X-linked recessive cause of episodic, oxidant-triggered haemolytic anaemia. G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway; it generates NADPH, which keeps glutathione reduced and shields the red cell from oxidative injury. The assay confirms deficiency, but its timing is critical because it can read falsely normal during an acute crisis.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Requested to investigate episodic haemolysis, neonatal jaundice, favism, or unexplained anaemia after an oxidant exposure — and to screen before high-risk drugs. Without NADPH-maintained glutathione, oxidants overwhelm the red cell, denaturing haemoglobin into Heinz bodies; splenic macrophages pluck these out, producing bite cells.

Commonest human enzymopathy; highest prevalence in African, Mediterranean, Middle-Eastern and South-East Asian ancestry.
X-linked recessive — classically symptomatic in males; heterozygous females can be affected via lyonisation.
Mediterranean variant is more severe than the African (A−) variant.
🫘Fava beans
Favism — classic dietary trigger
💊Primaquine
Antimalarials incl. tafenoquine
💊Dapsone
Also sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin
🦠Infection
Commonest overall precipitant
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

An EDTA venous sample is taken. The quantitative spectrophotometric assay measures the rate of NADP⁺→NADPH conversion (rise in absorbance at 340 nm), reported in IU/gHb. Rapid fluorescent-spot screening tests are used as a qualitative first pass.

Send blood film alongside — bite cells, blister cells and Heinz bodies (supravital stain) support the diagnosis in a crisis.
Reticulocyte count and haemolysis screen (↑LDH, ↑unconjugated bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin) contextualise the result.
Timing is everything — the assay is best deferred until steady state.
3INTERPRETATION

Activity is compared against the laboratory reference range and expressed as a percentage of normal.

Activity <10% of normal→Severe (Class I–II) deficiency — risk of significant haemolysis
Activity ~10–60% of normal→Partial deficiency (e.g. A− variant or heterozygous female)
Oxidant drug/fava bean + acute anaemia→Intravascular haemolysis: haemoglobinuria, jaundice, bite cells
Normal assay during a crisis→Cannot exclude deficiency — repeat after recovery
4PITFALLS & SAFETY

The central trap is the falsely normal assay in acute haemolysis. The oldest, most enzyme-depleted cells lyse first; the surviving young red cells and the reticulocytes released in response are enzyme-rich, so the measured average activity is spuriously raised.

Retest 2–3 months after recovery once the reticulocytosis has settled.
Recent transfusion also masks deficiency — donor cells have normal enzyme.
🚩 A NORMAL G6PD assay taken DURING an acute crisis does NOT exclude deficiency — young reticulocytes carry high enzyme and mask it, so always repeat weeks after recovery. Screen G6PD status BEFORE prescribing primaquine, rasburicase, dapsone or high-dose sulfonamides, and counsel patients to avoid fava beans and oxidant drugs.
🎓 Blood film buzzwords: bite cells and Heinz bodies (seen on supravital methyl-violet staining, not routine Romanowsky) point straight to G6PD deficiency. Contrast with hereditary spherocytosis (spherocytes, positive osmotic fragility) — both cause haemolysis but the film and family history differ.

HFE genotyping is the confirmatory genetic test for hereditary haemochromatosis, an autosomal recessive disorder of iron overload. It is not a first-line test: abnormal iron studies (a raised transferrin saturation together with a raised ferritin) come first, and only then is the patient tested for the two key HFE mutations, C282Y and H63D. Excess iron is deposited in the liver, pancreas, heart, joints and pituitary, and the condition is eminently treatable by venesection if caught early.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

The HFE protein normally regulates hepcidin, the master hormone that restrains intestinal iron absorption. Loss-of-function HFE mutations lower hepcidin, so the gut absorbs iron unchecked and total body iron rises progressively over decades.

Test when iron studies are persistently abnormal (raised ferritin and raised transferrin saturation).
Test first-degree relatives of a confirmed case (autosomal recessive, so siblings are highest risk).
Consider in unexplained cirrhosis, early arthropathy (2nd/3rd MCP joints), diabetes with bronze skin, or cardiomyopathy.
🧬C282Y
Major mutation; homozygosity is the classic disease genotype
🧬H63D
Minor mutation; causes overload mainly as C282Y/H63D compound heterozygote
🧪Ferritin
Marker of total iron stores, but an acute-phase reactant
🩸Transferrin sat.
Most specific early marker of iron overload
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Biochemistry first: fasting morning sample for transferrin saturation and ferritin (fasting reduces diet-related variation).
If both are raised on a confirmed repeat sample, send an EDTA blood sample for HFE genotyping (targeted PCR for C282Y and H63D).
Assess liver damage: LFTs, and if ferritin >1000 µg/L or LFTs abnormal, arrange liver assessment (MRI iron quantification ± biopsy) to look for cirrhosis.
Offer genetic counselling and cascade screening of first-degree relatives.
3INTERPRETATION
Transferrin saturation >45–50% + raised ferritin→Iron overload likely — proceed to HFE genotyping
C282Y homozygote→Genetically confirmed hereditary haemochromatosis
C282Y / H63D compound heterozygote→Overload possible, usually milder — interpret with iron studies
Simple C282Y or H63D heterozygote→Carrier — rarely causes significant overload; seek another cause
Ferritin >1000 µg/L→High cirrhosis risk — formal liver assessment needed
4PITFALLS, SAFETY & TREATMENT
A raised ferritin alone is not specific — it also rises with inflammation, alcohol excess, malignancy and metabolic (fatty liver) disease.
A normal HFE genotype does not exclude non-HFE (rarer) iron overload if iron studies are convincingly high.
Treatment: regular venesection to deplete iron stores (target ferritin, then maintenance), which normalises life expectancy if started before cirrhosis. Avoid iron and vitamin C supplements and excess alcohol.
🚩 Do not genotype on a raised ferritin alone — ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, so confirm with a raised transferrin saturation first. Miss the diagnosis and irreversible cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma may develop; always screen first-degree relatives, as early venesection is curative-quality prevention.
🎓 The single highest-yield fact: C282Y homozygosity is the classic genotype of hereditary haemochromatosis. Remember the triad of bronze skin + diabetes + hepatomegaly ("bronze diabetes"), and that transferrin saturation is the most useful early screening test.

Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of the copper-transporting ATPase ATP7B, in which failure of biliary copper excretion and copper incorporation into caeruloplasmin causes toxic copper accumulation in the liver, brain (especially the basal ganglia) and eyes. It is a rare but crucial diagnosis: it presents in young people (typically 5–35 years) with liver disease, movement disorders or psychiatric change, and it is fatal if untreated yet eminently treatable if caught early. Diagnosis rests on a pattern of biochemical and ophthalmological findings rather than a single test.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

ATP7B is a hepatocyte copper-transporting ATPase that performs two jobs: loading copper onto apo-caeruloplasmin, and exporting excess copper into bile. When ATP7B is defective, copper is neither excreted nor bound, so unbound (free) copper spills into the blood and deposits in tissues, generating oxidative injury.

Liver: fatty change → chronic hepatitis → cirrhosis; may present as acute (fulminant) liver failure.
Brain / basal ganglia: tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, parkinsonism, and neuropsychiatric change (depression, personality change, psychosis).
Eyes: copper in Descemet membrane produces Kayser-Fleischer rings.

Consider it in any young patient with unexplained liver disease, a movement disorder, or new psychiatric illness with hepatic clues.

2HOW THE WORK-UP IS PERFORMED

There is no single confirmatory blood test; diagnosis combines several investigations, often scored with the Leipzig criteria.

Serum caeruloplasmin — low because copper-free apo-caeruloplasmin is degraded faster.
24-hour urinary copper — collected in a copper-free container; reflects the raised free copper pool.
Slit-lamp examination — by an ophthalmologist to detect Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Liver biopsy for hepatic copper quantification when non-invasive tests are equivocal.
ATP7B gene sequencing confirms the diagnosis and enables family screening.

A penicillamine-challenge urinary copper test is sometimes used in children to boost sensitivity.

3INTERPRETATION — CUT-OFFS
Serum caeruloplasmin < 0.2 g/L (<20 mg/dL)→Strongly supportive of Wilson disease
24-hour urinary copper > 1.6 µmol/24h (>100 µg/24h)→Diagnostic-range copper excretion (>0.6 µmol/24h is abnormal)
Hepatic copper > 4 µmol/g dry weight (>250 µg/g)→Confirms hepatic copper overload
Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit lamp→Present in nearly all neuro cases; strongly supportive
Two pathogenic ATP7B mutations→Confirms diagnosis; guides family screening
Low ALP with high bilirubin; ALP:bilirubin ratio < 4→Clue to Wilsonian fulminant liver failure
4PITFALLS, TREATMENT & SAFETY

Pitfalls: caeruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant, so it can be falsely normal in inflammation, pregnancy or oestrogen use; and low levels also occur in heterozygous carriers and in aceruloplasminaemia. KF rings may be absent in patients presenting with liver disease alone.

🧪Penicillamine
First-line chelator; watch for marrow, renal and neuro worsening
🧪Trientine
Alternative chelator, better tolerated
🧪Zinc
Blocks gut copper absorption; maintenance / pre-symptomatic
🧪Liver transplant
Curative for fulminant failure or decompensated cirrhosis
🚩 Consider Wilson disease in ANY person under 40 with unexplained liver disease combined with a movement disorder or new neuropsychiatric symptoms — it is treatable but fatal if missed. Fulminant Wilsonian liver failure (often with Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia and a low ALP:bilirubin ratio) is a medical emergency requiring urgent transplant assessment.
🎓 The classic triad for exams: low serum caeruloplasmin + Kayser-Fleischer rings + raised 24-hour urinary copper in a young patient with liver or neuropsychiatric disease. KF rings plus low caeruloplasmin is enough to make the diagnosis highly likely.

α1-Antitrypsin (A1AT) Pi phenotyping is a laboratory test that classifies which A1AT protein variants a patient carries, confirming the diagnosis of α1-antitrypsin deficiency in a patient with a low serum A1AT level. A1AT is a protease inhibitor that shields the lung from neutrophil elastase; the severe-deficiency PiZZ phenotype predisposes to early-onset panacinar (basal) emphysema and to liver disease, and phenotyping identifies exactly which alleles are present so risk can be stratified and family members screened.

1Indication & principle

A1AT is encoded by the SERPINA1 gene and inherited in an autosomal co-dominant fashion — both alleles are expressed, so the phenotype reflects the combination inherited. The normal allele is M; the common deficiency alleles are S and Z. The Z mutation causes the protein to misfold and polymerise, so it is retained within hepatocytes rather than secreted — this simultaneously lowers circulating A1AT (loss of anti-elastase protection in the lung) and causes toxic accumulation in the liver.

Test is triggered when a low serum A1AT level is found, or in young patients with unexplained emphysema, basal-predominant COPD, or unexplained liver disease/cirrhosis.
Uninhibited neutrophil elastase digests alveolar elastin → loss of elastic recoil → panacinar emphysema, characteristically at the lung bases.
2How it is performed

Step 1 is quantitative: measure the serum A1AT concentration (normal reference roughly 1.1–2.1 g/L). A low result prompts step 2 — characterising the variants:

Phenotyping by isoelectric focusing separates M, S and Z proteins by their charge to reveal the Pi (protease inhibitor) type.
Genotyping (PCR for the S and Z alleles) is increasingly used to confirm the result and is unaffected by inflammation.

Interpret alongside a concurrent CRP, because A1AT is an acute-phase reactant; ideally sample when the patient is well.

3Interpretation
PiMM (normal)→Normal A1AT level; no increased risk
PiMZ (heterozygous carrier)→Intermediate level (~60% normal); small excess risk, especially if smoker
PiSZ→Moderate deficiency (~40% normal); intermediate lung risk
PiZZ (homozygous)→Severe deficiency (~10–15% normal); high risk of emphysema & liver disease
Serum A1AT < 0.5 g/L→Below protective threshold — consistent with severe deficiency, phenotype to confirm
🧬M allele
Normal, fully functional A1AT
🧪S allele
Mild reduction in A1AT level
🫁Z allele
Misfolds & polymerises; severe deficiency
🩺PiZZ
Basal emphysema + hepatocyte injury
4Pitfalls & management context
A single quantitative level can mislead — inflammation raises it (false reassurance), so always confirm the variant by phenotyping/genotyping.
Liver disease is caused by the gain-of-function accumulation of polymerised Z protein in hepatocytes, so it is not prevented by avoiding smoking (unlike the lung disease).
Confirmed PiZZ warrants smoking-cessation support, screening of first-degree relatives, and monitoring of lung and liver function.
🚩 Smoking dramatically accelerates lung destruction in A1AT deficiency — cigarette smoke both inactivates residual A1AT and recruits neutrophils, so a PiZZ smoker can develop disabling emphysema by their 30s–40s. Also beware: because A1AT is an acute-phase reactant, the serum level may be spuriously normal during infection or inflammation, masking the deficiency.
🎓 Classic exam trigger: a young non-smoker (or light smoker) with basal (lower-zone) panacinar emphysema plus deranged LFTs or cirrhosis — think PiZZ α1-antitrypsin deficiency and request phenotyping.

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the commonest inherited kidney disorder (~1 in 800–1000) and a leading genetic cause of end-stage renal failure (ESRF). Progressive bilateral cyst formation destroys nephrons, causing hypertension, haematuria, loin pain and declining GFR, alongside extrarenal features. Two genes account for almost all cases: PKD1 (chromosome 16, encoding polycystin-1) and PKD2 (chromosome 4, encoding polycystin-2).

1GENETICS & PRINCIPLE

ADPKD is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern: each child of an affected parent has a 50% risk, and penetrance is essentially complete by old age. The polycystin proteins localise to the primary cilium of tubular epithelial cells, where they act as a mechanosensory calcium-signalling complex regulating tubular diameter. Loss of function disrupts intracellular calcium and cAMP handling, driving fluid secretion and epithelial proliferation that expand fluid-filled cysts.

🧬PKD1
Chromosome 16; encodes polycystin-1; ~85% of cases; more severe
🧬PKD2
Chromosome 4; encodes polycystin-2; ~15%; milder, later ESRF
🔬Polycystin-1
Large membrane receptor; mechanosensor on the primary cilium
🔬Polycystin-2
Calcium-permeable cation channel; partners with polycystin-1
2DIAGNOSIS — ULTRASOUND CRITERIA

In a patient with a positive family history, diagnosis is usually made by renal ultrasound using age-related cyst counts (Ravine / unified Pei criteria), because cyst number rises with age. Genetic testing is reserved for equivocal scans, younger potential living-related kidney donors needing to be excluded, or reproductive counselling.

Age 15–39 with family history→≥3 cysts (unilateral or bilateral) is diagnostic
Age 40–59 with family history→≥2 cysts in EACH kidney is diagnostic
Age ≥60 with family history→≥4 cysts in each kidney is diagnostic
Age <40, negative scan, potential donor→Ultrasound cannot exclude — use genetic testing
3PKD1 vs PKD2 — INTERPRETING THE GENOTYPE

Genotype strongly predicts prognosis. PKD1 disease is more severe with earlier and heavier cyst burden, while PKD2 runs a milder course with kidney survival roughly 20 years longer.

PKD1 mutation→Median ESRF ~54–58 years; more/larger cysts, earlier hypertension
PKD2 mutation→Median ESRF ~74–79 years; some never reach ESRF
Extrarenal: hepatic (polycystic liver) cysts — the commonest extrarenal manifestation, usually preserving liver function.
Berry (intracranial saccular) aneurysms in the circle of Willis, risking subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Mitral valve prolapse and other valve disease; also pancreatic and seminal-vesicle cysts.
Hypertension is early and near-universal, driven by activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.
4PITFALLS & MANAGEMENT CAVEATS

Ultrasound has poor negative predictive value in young at-risk people, so a normal scan under 40 does not exclude disease — critical when clearing a living donor. A few simple renal cysts are common and age-related, so cyst counts must be matched to age to avoid over-diagnosis. Tolvaptan (a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist) may slow progression in rapidly progressive disease but causes aquaresis and requires liver monitoring.

🚩 ADPKD carries an increased risk of intracranial berry aneurysm and subarachnoid haemorrhage. Screen with MR angiography if there is a family history of SAH or aneurysm, a previous rupture, or high-risk occupations. A thunderclap headache in an ADPKD patient is a ruptured aneurysm until proven otherwise. Treat hypertension aggressively — an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is first-line, targeting ≤130/80 mmHg to protect kidney and cardiovascular outcomes.
🎓 Remember: PKD1 is worse (more severe, earlier ESRF) — think "1 is the bad one." PKD1 accounts for ~85% of cases and reaches ESRF around two decades earlier than PKD2.
GENETICS / MOLECULAR__Cancer & Endocrine:
The RET proto-oncogene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase; a germline activating (gain-of-function) mutation causes Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN2). RET testing is a genetic investigation that confirms the diagnosis in an index case, screens at-risk relatives, and — crucially — stratifies the timing of prophylactic total thyroidectomy before medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) develops. Nearly all mutation carriers will develop MTC if untreated, so RET status directly drives a life-saving surgical decision.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Test the germline RET sequence (peripheral blood DNA) to identify carriers who need surveillance and pre-emptive surgery. The three phenotypes are:

🧪MEN2A
MTC + phaeochromocytoma + primary hyperparathyroidism (commonest, ~95% of MEN2)
🧬MEN2B
MTC + phaeochromocytoma + mucosal neuromas + marfanoid habitus (NO hyperparathyroidism); most aggressive MTC
🦋FMTC
Familial MTC alone, without phaeo or parathyroid disease

RET is also somatically mutated in a subset of sporadic MTC, but that is acquired and non-heritable — germline testing distinguishes hereditary disease requiring family screening.

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Sample: EDTA blood for germline DNA; targeted RET exon sequencing (classically codons in exons 10, 11, 13–16).
Index case: anyone with MTC, MEN2 phenotype, or a suggestive family history is offered testing after genetic counselling and consent.
Cascade screening: once the family mutation is known, at-risk relatives (including infants) are offered predictive testing so carriers can be identified before disease.
Tumour marker: serum calcitonin (and CEA) is the biochemical marker of MTC — used alongside RET for monitoring and post-operative follow-up.
3INTERPRETATION — MUTATION GUIDES TIMING

The specific codon predicts MTC aggressiveness, which sets the risk category and the age for prophylactic total thyroidectomy:

Codon M918T (MEN2B) — HIGHEST risk→Thyroidectomy in the first year of life (infancy)
Codon C634 (classic MEN2A) — HIGH risk→Thyroidectomy by age ~5 years (or earlier if calcitonin rises)
Moderate-risk codons (e.g. 609, 611, 618, 620, 768, 804)→Surgery timed by calcitonin surveillance, often after age 5
Rising / elevated serum calcitonin in a carrier→Evidence of MTC — brings surgery forward
Positive predictive test in an asymptomatic child→Enter MTC surveillance + plan prophylactic thyroidectomy
4PITFALLS & SAFETY
A negative predictive test in a relative is only reliable once the family-specific mutation has been identified in the index case.
MEN2 is autosomal dominant — each child of a carrier has a 50% risk; de novo mutations are common in MEN2B, so absent family history does not exclude it.
Do not overlook the associated tumours: screen carriers periodically for phaeochromocytoma (plasma/urine metanephrines) and, in MEN2A, hyperparathyroidism (calcium, PTH).
🚩 ALWAYS exclude and treat phaeochromocytoma BEFORE any surgery in MEN2 — including prophylactic thyroidectomy. Anaesthesia or operating on an unrecognised phaeo can precipitate a fatal hypertensive crisis. Screen with plasma/urinary metanephrines; if positive, resect the phaeo first with adequate alpha- then beta-blockade.
🎓 High-yield: MEN2B carries the most aggressive MTC and the earliest neuromuscular/marfanoid clues (mucosal neuromas on lips/tongue, thickened corneal nerves) — it mandates thyroidectomy in infancy, whereas MEN2A/C634 is typically operated by age 5. Remember MEN2B lacks hyperparathyroidism.

MEN1 gene sequencing is a germline genetic test that identifies inactivating mutations in the MEN1 tumour-suppressor gene (encoding the protein menin) on chromosome 11q13. It confirms the diagnosis of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 — an autosomal dominant syndrome defined by the "3 Ps": Parathyroid hyperplasia, Pancreatic/GI neuroendocrine tumours and Pituitary adenomas — and enables lifelong biochemical and imaging surveillance of the index case and at-risk relatives.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Menin is a tumour suppressor; a germline loss-of-function mutation in one allele, followed by somatic loss of the second allele (Knudson two-hit) in endocrine tissue, drives tumour formation. Because inheritance is autosomal dominant, each first-degree relative of a carrier has a 50% risk. Testing is offered to establish the diagnosis and to cascade-screen family members so that surveillance can begin before tumours become symptomatic.

Clinical MEN1 = any 2 of the 3 characteristic tumour types (parathyroid, entero-pancreatic, pituitary).
Familial MEN1 = one MEN1 tumour plus a first-degree relative with confirmed MEN1.
A pathogenic germline variant is identifiable in roughly 80%–90% of clinically diagnosed families.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A peripheral venous EDTA blood sample provides germline DNA (from leucocytes). The whole coding region and splice sites of the MEN1 gene are analysed by next-generation or Sanger sequencing, with multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) to detect large deletions. Genetic counselling and informed consent precede testing.

Index (proband) testing first — identify the family-specific mutation.
Predictive (cascade) testing of relatives then targets that known variant only.
Carrier surveillance from childhood: annual calcium/PTH, gut hormones (gastrin, glucose/insulin), prolactin/IGF-1, plus periodic pancreatic and pituitary MRI.
3INTERPRETATION — THE 3 Ps

A pathogenic variant confirms MEN1 and mandates surveillance; the phenotype is dominated by three organ systems.

Parathyroid hyperplasia→Primary hyperparathyroidism — commonest & earliest (~90% by age 50); ↑calcium with ↑/inappropriately normal PTH
Pancreatic / GI NET→Gastrinoma → Zollinger-Ellison (fasting gastrin >10× normal, gastric pH <2); insulinoma → fasting hypoglycaemia
Pituitary adenoma→Prolactinoma most common → ↑prolactin, galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea/hypogonadism
🧪Parathyroid
Four-gland hyperplasia; hypercalcaemia is usually the first biochemical clue.
🧪Pancreas / GI
Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) and insulinoma; leading cause of MEN1 mortality.
🧪Pituitary
Prolactinoma commonest; may cause mass effect and visual field loss.
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
A negative result in a clinically definite family may reflect a mutation missed by current methods — it does not exclude MEN1 unless the family mutation is known and absent.
Variants of uncertain significance require expert interpretation and cannot be used to reassure relatives.
De novo mutations occur (~10%), so a negative family history does not rule out the diagnosis.
Penetrance is age-related and expression variable — carriers need surveillance even while asymptomatic.
🚩 Recurrent, multi-gland or familial primary hyperparathyroidism, or a gastrinoma at a young age, should prompt MEN1 gene testing. Confirmed carriers require lifelong biochemical and imaging surveillance — missed pancreatic NETs are the main cause of premature death in MEN1.
🎓 Remember the 3 Ps — Parathyroid (first & commonest), Pancreas, Pituitary. Contrast with MEN2 (medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma, parathyroid) driven by the RET proto-oncogene.

Germline testing in urological cancers identifies inherited mutations that change prognosis, guide targeted therapy, and trigger surveillance of the patient and their relatives. In prostate cancer, DNA-repair genes (BRCA2, BRCA1, ATM) mark aggressive disease and predict response to PARP inhibitors and platinum. In renal cancer, three syndromes dominate exams: VHL (clear cell RCC), FLCN (Birt-Hogg-Dubé) and FH (hereditary leiomyomatosis & aggressive papillary RCC).

1INDICATION — who to test and why it matters

Germline (inherited) variants are present in every cell and are found via a blood or saliva sample, distinct from somatic tumour-only mutations. Testing is offered when the personal or family history suggests an inherited predisposition, because a positive result alters treatment, cancer surveillance, and cascade testing of relatives.

Prostate: metastatic or high-risk disease, or strong family history → test DNA-repair genes (BRCA2, BRCA1, ATM, and others).
Renal: young age (typically <46 yrs), bilateral or multifocal tumours, syndromic features, or a suggestive family history → refer for germline testing.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Pre-test genetic counselling explains the implications of a result for the patient and family. A germline sample (blood/saliva) undergoes gene-panel sequencing; results are returned as pathogenic, benign, or a variant of uncertain significance (VUS). Confirmed pathogenic variants prompt cascade testing of at-risk relatives and enrolment in surveillance programmes.

Germline panels differ from somatic tumour testing, which guides therapy but is not inherited.
A VUS is not actionable and should not drive treatment or surveillance decisions.
3INTERPRETATION — gene to tumour

Each gene maps to a characteristic tumour spectrum and management implication.

BRCA2 (prostate)→Aggressive, higher-grade disease; predicts PARP inhibitor (olaparib) & platinum response
BRCA1 / ATM (prostate)→Increased risk / aggressive disease; ATM a weaker PARP predictor than BRCA2
VHL→Clear cell RCC + phaeochromocytoma, CNS/retinal haemangioblastoma, pancreatic & renal cysts
FLCN (Birt-Hogg-Dubé)→Chromophobe RCC / oncocytoma, lung cysts & spontaneous pneumothorax, skin fibrofolliculomas
FH (HLRCC)→Aggressive papillary type 2 RCC + cutaneous & uterine leiomyomas
🧬BRCA2
Aggressive prostate cancer; PARP & platinum sensitive
🩸VHL
Clear cell RCC, phaeo, haemangioblastoma, retinal angioma
🫁FLCN
Chromophobe/oncocytoma, lung cysts/pneumothorax, skin fibrofolliculomas
🔥FH
Aggressive papillary type 2 RCC; cutaneous & uterine leiomyomas
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
A VUS can cause anxiety and inappropriate intervention if over-interpreted — do not act on it.
FH-associated papillary type 2 RCC metastasises early even when small; nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy is generally avoided in favour of wide excision.
Germline results have implications for relatives and for insurance/psychological wellbeing — counselling and consent are essential.
🚩 Young, bilateral or multifocal RCC, or a strong family history of RCC/syndromic features → refer for germline testing and enrol in lifelong tumour surveillance. Never treat these as sporadic single tumours.
🎓 High-yield: metastatic prostate cancer with a germline BRCA2 mutation → PARP inhibitor (olaparib). BRCA2 tumours are more aggressive but exquisitely sensitive to PARP inhibition and platinum chemotherapy.

BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumour-suppressor genes encoding proteins essential for repairing DNA double-strand breaks by homologous recombination. Germline pathogenic variants are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and dramatically raise lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer. Identifying carriers allows enhanced surveillance, risk-reducing surgery, chemoprevention and access to PARP-inhibitor therapy that exploits the tumour's repair defect.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE — why we test

BRCA1/2 proteins guard genomic integrity: when both alleles are lost, cells cannot faithfully repair double-strand breaks and accumulate mutations, driving carcinogenesis (a classic two-hit tumour-suppressor mechanism). Testing is a germline blood/saliva DNA analysis to find heritable pathogenic variants that explain a high-risk phenotype and enable cascade testing of relatives.

🧬BRCA1 (17q)
High breast & ovarian risk; strongly linked to triple-negative breast cancer
🧬BRCA2 (13q)
High breast & ovarian risk; also male breast, prostate & pancreatic cancer
🔧HR repair
Error-free double-strand break repair using the sister chromatid as template
👪Cascade
First-degree relatives have a 50% chance of inheriting a known variant
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — who qualifies & the pathway

Referral to clinical genetics for pre-test counselling, then a germline DNA test (blood or saliva). UK/NICE practice uses a family-history risk threshold (a combined BRCA carrier probability of ≥10%) to offer testing. Where an affected relative carries a known variant, targeted single-variant testing is used; otherwise full gene sequencing is performed.

Young-onset breast cancer (diagnosed under ~40–50 years)
Triple-negative breast cancer, especially under 60
Male breast cancer at any age
High-grade non-mucinous epithelial ovarian cancer at any age
Bilateral breast cancer or multiple affected close relatives
Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry (three common founder variants)
3INTERPRETATION — risk & the numbers

A pathogenic/likely-pathogenic variant confirms high risk and drives management. A “variant of uncertain significance” (VUS) is not actionable and should not trigger surgery. A negative result in a family with a known variant is truly reassuring (population-level risk), whereas a negative full-gene test in an untested family does not exclude other predisposition.

Lifetime breast cancer risk (BRCA1/2 carrier)→Greatly raised, up to ~70% (vs ~12–15% population)
Lifetime ovarian cancer risk→~40–60% (BRCA1) and ~10–20% (BRCA2)
BRCA1 breast tumour phenotype→Frequently triple-negative (ER−, PR−, HER2−), high grade
Confirmed pathogenic variant→Offer surveillance, risk-reducing surgery, chemoprevention, cascade testing
Variant of uncertain significance (VUS)→Manage by family history only; do NOT base surgery on it
4MANAGEMENT, PITFALLS & THERAPY

Carriers are offered annual breast MRI surveillance (more sensitive than mammography in dense young breast tissue, typically from age 30), risk-reducing bilateral mastectomy, and risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (BSO) once childbearing is complete. Chemoprevention (e.g. tamoxifen) may be offered. There is no reliable ovarian screening test, which is why surgery is central to ovarian risk reduction.

Enhanced MRI screening detects cancers earlier but cannot prevent them
Risk-reducing mastectomy cuts breast cancer risk by ~90–95%
BSO before natural menopause induces surgical menopause — counsel re HRT
PARP inhibitors (olaparib) treat BRCA-mutant breast, ovarian, prostate & pancreatic cancer
🚩 Risk-reducing bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy lowers BOTH ovarian AND breast cancer risk (via oestrogen withdrawal) and is the single most effective intervention for ovarian risk, since no ovarian screening reliably detects early disease. Always arrange cascade genetic testing of at-risk relatives — each first-degree relative has a 50% chance of carrying the variant and identifying them enables prevention.
🎓 PARP inhibitors work by synthetic lethality: PARP repairs single-strand breaks; blocking it forces reliance on homologous recombination, which BRCA-mutant tumour cells cannot perform, so unrepaired damage becomes lethal double-strand breaks — killing the cancer while sparing normal (HR-competent) cells.

The BRAF test is a somatic (tumour) molecular test that looks for an activating point mutation in the BRAF gene — overwhelmingly V600E (and less often V600K). BRAF is a kinase in the RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK (MAPK) growth pathway; a V600 mutation locks the kinase permanently “on”, driving constant proliferation. A positive result does not just describe the cancer — it selects treatment, unlocking BRAF-inhibitor + MEK-inhibitor targeted therapy in advanced melanoma, and carrying prognostic and diagnostic meaning in colorectal, thyroid and haematological cancers.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

BRAF sits downstream of RAS and upstream of MEK/ERK. The V600E substitution (valine → glutamate at codon 600) mimics phosphorylation, giving constitutive kinase activity independent of upstream signals — a classic oncogenic driver mutation.

Found in roughly 40–50% of cutaneous melanomas, typically younger patients and intermittently sun-exposed skin.
It is a somatic (acquired, tumour-only) mutation — not inherited — so testing is done on tumour tissue, not a germline blood test.
Also tested in colorectal cancer, papillary thyroid carcinoma and hairy cell leukaemia, where it carries prognostic or diagnostic value.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Testing is performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour tissue from a biopsy or resection, once a cancer diagnosis is confirmed on histology.

Molecular methods: real-time PCR / allele-specific PCR, next-generation sequencing (NGS panels), or pyrosequencing to detect the V600 variant.
Immunohistochemistry with the VE1 antibody can rapidly detect the V600E protein but a positive/equivocal result is usually confirmed by a molecular assay.
Adequate viable tumour cellularity is needed; heavily necrotic or scanty samples may give false negatives and require repeat sampling.
3INTERPRETATION

The result is binary in impact — mutation present or absent — but its meaning depends on the tumour type.

BRAF V600E/V600K positive in advanced melanoma→eligible for BRAF inhibitor + MEK inhibitor targeted therapy
BRAF wild-type melanoma→BRAF inhibitors ineffective; use immunotherapy (checkpoint inhibitors)
BRAF V600E in colorectal cancer→poorer prognosis; predicts resistance to anti-EGFR monotherapy
BRAF V600E + loss of MLH1 in colorectal cancer→favours sporadic MMR-deficiency; helps exclude Lynch syndrome
BRAF V600E in papillary thyroid / hairy cell leukaemia→supports diagnosis; hairy cell leukaemia is almost universally BRAF-mutated
🧬V600E
commonest variant; valine→glutamate, drives MAPK
💊BRAF inhibitor
vemurafenib / dabrafenib block mutant kinase
🔗MEK inhibitor
trametinib; added to prevent paradoxical activation
🔬VE1 IHC
rapid antibody screen for V600E protein
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
A negative result may be a false negative from low tumour content — correlate with sample adequacy before excluding a mutation.
Acquired resistance to BRAF/MEK inhibitors develops over months as tumours reactivate the MAPK pathway; response is often not durable as monotherapy.
Non-V600 BRAF variants exist and may not respond to V600-directed inhibitors, so the specific variant matters.
🚩 BRAF-inhibitor monotherapy can trigger paradoxical activation of the MAPK pathway in BRAF wild-type cells, causing secondary skin malignancies (cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas and keratoacanthomas). This is why a BRAF inhibitor is combined with a MEK inhibitor, which suppresses the downstream pathway and improves efficacy.
🎓 Advanced BRAF V600E-positive melanoma → treat with a BRAF inhibitor PLUS a MEK inhibitor (e.g. dabrafenib + trametinib). Wild-type melanoma gets immunotherapy instead — a favourite exam distinction.
GENETICS / MOLECULAR__Neuro, Connective:
Neurogenetic testing uses molecular diagnostics to confirm inherited disorders of the nervous system and muscle. Most classic exam entities are either trinucleotide repeat expansions (Huntington, myotonic dystrophy), large-gene deletions/duplications (Duchenne dystrophin, CMT1A), or dominant tumour-suppressor conditions (NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis). The test both confirms the diagnosis and enables cascade/predictive testing of relatives – which carries heavy counselling implications.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE
Testing is requested to confirm a clinical suspicion, to clarify inheritance risk, or for predictive (presymptomatic) testing in an at-risk relative. Repeat-expansion disorders show anticipation – the repeat lengthens through generations, so the disease appears earlier and more severely in successive offspring, especially with the CTG expansion of myotonic dystrophy. Deletion disorders such as Duchenne disrupt the reading frame of the dystrophin gene, whereas Becker keeps it in-frame and is milder.
Repeat expansion → Huntington (CAG), myotonic dystrophy (CTG).
Deletion / duplication → Duchenne/Becker (dystrophin), CMT1A (PMP22).
Tumour suppressor → NF1, NF2, TSC1/TSC2.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
A peripheral venous EDTA blood sample provides genomic DNA. Repeat lengths are sized by PCR (with Southern blot or triplet-primed PCR for very large expansions), while dystrophin and PMP22 dosage changes are detected by MLPA (multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification) or array CGH. NF1, NF2 and TSC are analysed by gene sequencing plus deletion/duplication analysis. Predictive testing for Huntington is only done through a structured multi-visit genetic-counselling pathway, not on a single clinic visit.
Serum creatine kinase (CK) is markedly raised (often >10× upper limit) in Duchenne and supports the request.
Cascade testing offers targeted analysis of the known familial variant to relatives.
3INTERPRETATION & CUT-OFFS
Interpretation maps the molecular result onto the specific disease and, for expansions, onto the repeat number.
HTT CAG ≥40→Huntington disease (fully penetrant); 36–39 reduced penetrance; ≤26 normal
DMPK CTG expansion (>50, up to 1000s)→Myotonic dystrophy type 1
Dystrophin (DMD) out-of-frame deletion→Duchenne MD (X-linked); in-frame → Becker MD
PMP22 duplication (17p11.2)→Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A
NF1 mutation (17q11.2, neurofibromin)→Neurofibromatosis 1 (café-au-lait, Lisch nodules)
NF2 mutation (22q, merlin)→Neurofibromatosis 2 (bilateral vestibular schwannomas)
TSC1 or TSC2 mutation→Tuberous sclerosis (hamartin / tuberin)
4PITFALLS & SAFETY
Repeat sizing near thresholds is uncertain: intermediate CAG alleles (27–35) do not cause disease in the carrier but may expand in offspring. A negative deletion screen in suspected Duchenne does not exclude the diagnosis – point mutations need sequencing. Mosaicism (common in NF2 and TSC) can give a normal blood result despite affected tissue. Predictive results affect insurance, reproductive choices and mental health, so must be delivered with support.
🧠HTT CAG
Huntington; AD; anticipation
💪Dystrophin
Duchenne/Becker; X-linked; high CK
🔒DMPK CTG
Myotonic dystrophy; grip myotonia
🦶PMP22
CMT1A duplication; pes cavus
🟤NF1 / NF2
Neurofibromin / merlin
🌱TSC1 / TSC2
Hamartin / tuberin; hamartomas
🚩 Predictive (presymptomatic) testing for Huntington disease must never be done casually: there is no cure, results carry profound psychological, reproductive and insurance implications, and testing of asymptomatic minors is not permitted. It proceeds only through a formal, multi-session genetic-counselling protocol with informed consent.
🎓 Remember CAG = Huntington (≥40 repeats, autosomal dominant) and that repeat-expansion disorders show anticipation – earlier onset and greater severity down the generations.

The heritable connective tissue disorders are a group of autosomal dominant conditions in which a mutation in a single structural-protein gene weakens the extracellular matrix, producing recognisable multisystem syndromes. The three most examined are Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1), vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (type III collagen) and osteogenesis imperfecta (type I collagen). This subtab maps each gene to its protein, its disorder and the clinical clues that let you spot it, and flags the shared lethal complication: arterial dissection.

1THE PRINCIPLE — ONE GENE, ONE MATRIX PROTEIN, ONE SYNDROME

Connective tissue strength depends on a small number of large structural proteins. A mutation in the gene for any one of them weakens whichever tissues rely most heavily on that protein, so each disorder has a signature distribution of features. Most are autosomal dominant, so a single mutant allele is enough and there is typically an affected parent, though new (de novo) mutations are common.

FBN1 (fibrillin-1)→Marfan syndrome — skeleton, eye (lens), aorta
COL3A1 (type III collagen)→Vascular Ehlers-Danlos — arteries, bowel, uterus, skin
COL1A1 / COL1A2 (type I collagen)→Osteogenesis imperfecta — bone, sclera, teeth, hearing
🧬FBN1
Fibrillin-1 microfibrils; loss of TGF-β sequestration → Marfan
🩸COL3A1
Type III collagen of hollow organs & vessel walls → vascular EDS
🦴COL1A1/2
Type I collagen of bone & sclera → osteogenesis imperfecta
2MARFAN SYNDROME (FBN1) — THE TALL PHENOTYPE

Fibrillin-1 forms the microfibrils that scaffold elastic tissue and normally sequester TGF-β. Defective fibrillin releases excess TGF-β signalling, driving overgrowth and matrix weakness. Diagnosis uses the revised Ghent criteria, which weight the aortic root and the lens most heavily.

Skeleton: tall stature, long limbs, arm span > height, arachnodactyly (positive wrist/thumb signs), pectus deformity, scoliosis, high-arched palate, joint hypermobility.
Eye: ectopia lentis — lens dislocation classically upwards (superotemporal), a near-specific Marfan clue.
Cardiovascular: aortic root dilatation, aortic regurgitation, dissection; mitral valve prolapse.
Aortic root Z-score ≥ 2 + ectopia lentis→Diagnostic of Marfan (Ghent) even without family history
Lens dislocated upwards→Marfan (contrast: homocystinuria dislocates down)
🎓 High-yield hook: FBN1 = fibrillin = Marfan, and the aortic root is the number one killer. If a tall patient with long fingers and an upward lens dislocation appears, echo the aortic root.
3VASCULAR EDS (COL3A1) & OSTEOGENESIS IMPERFECTA (COL1A1/2)

Vascular Ehlers-Danlos (type IV) is caused by defective type III collagen, the collagen of arterial walls and hollow organs. It is the dangerous EDS subtype: patients present with translucent thin skin (visible veins), easy bruising, characteristic facies, and catastrophic spontaneous rupture of medium/large arteries, bowel or the gravid uterus. Joint hypermobility is often limited to small joints, so it lacks the dramatic skin stretchiness of classical EDS.

Thin translucent skin + spontaneous arterial or bowel rupture→Vascular EDS (COL3A1) until proven otherwise

Osteogenesis imperfecta results from defective type I collagen, the main protein of bone. Features are brittle bones with recurrent low-trauma fractures, blue sclerae (thin sclera revealing choroid), progressive conductive/mixed hearing loss, dentinogenesis imperfecta (opalescent teeth), ligamentous laxity and short stature. Severity ranges from mild (type I) to perinatal-lethal (type II).

Recurrent fractures + blue sclerae + early deafness→Osteogenesis imperfecta (COL1A1/COL1A2)
Blue sclerae in an infant with fractures must prompt OI on the differential for non-accidental injury.
Bisphosphonates reduce fracture rate in moderate-to-severe OI.
4SURVEILLANCE, PITFALLS & MANAGEMENT

Management centres on protecting the aorta and arteries and reducing fracture burden. Marfan and vascular EDS both need lifelong vascular imaging and lifestyle modification; OI needs bone protection and hearing review.

Marfan: serial echocardiography of the aortic root; beta-blockers or an ARB (losartan) to slow root dilatation; prophylactic aortic root replacement at threshold diameter; avoid isometric/contact sport.
Vascular EDS: avoid arteriography/invasive vascular procedures where possible (vessels tear); celiprolol reduces vascular events; treat ruptures as surgical emergencies with fragile-tissue precautions.
OI: bisphosphonates, fracture management, physiotherapy, audiology surveillance.
Marfan aortic root reaching ~5.0 cm (or lower with risk factors)→Refer for prophylactic root replacement
🚩 Marfan and vascular EDS both carry a lethal risk of aortic/arterial dissection or rupture — vascular EDS is the dangerous EDS subtype. Maintain aortic-root echo surveillance, use beta-blockers/ARB (celiprolol in vEDS), and advise avoidance of contact and isometric sport. Sudden chest, back or abdominal pain in these patients is dissection or rupture until excluded.

Cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) circulates in maternal plasma from ~7 weeks' gestation and lets us test the fetus non-invasively from a maternal blood sample. It underpins two prenatal uses: fetal RHD genotyping (does an RhD-negative mother actually need anti-D?) and non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) for the common aneuploidies. Where a definitive karyotype is required, invasive sampling — chorionic villus sampling (CVS) or amniocentesis — remains the diagnostic gold standard.

1Indication & principle

Fragments of placental (fetal) DNA are shed into the maternal circulation and mix with maternal cell-free DNA, forming ~5–20% of total plasma cfDNA. Sequencing or targeted PCR of this pool interrogates the fetal genotype without touching the fetus.

Fetal RHD genotyping: an RhD-negative mother lacks the RHD gene, so any RHD sequence detected in her plasma must be fetal — identifying the RhD-positive fetus that needs anti-D.
NIPT for aneuploidy: counts relative amounts of chromosome-specific fragments; an excess from chromosome 21, 18 or 13 signals a high chance of trisomy.
2How it is performed

Non-invasive tests need only a maternal venous blood sample; invasive tests sample the pregnancy directly under continuous ultrasound guidance.

Fetal RHD: maternal blood from ~11–16 weeks; offered routinely to RhD-negative women to target antenatal anti-D.
NIPT: maternal blood, usually from 10 weeks onward once fetal fraction is adequate.
CVS: transabdominal/transcervical placental biopsy at 11–14 weeks → rapid QF-PCR and karyotype/array.
Amniocentesis: aspiration of amniotic fluid at ≥15 weeks → QF-PCR, karyotype, microarray.
3Interpretation

Match each test to what its result actually means and the action it triggers.

Fetal RHD positive→give routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis to the RhD-negative mother
Fetal RHD negative→fetus RhD negative — anti-D can safely be withheld
NIPT “high chance”→screen positive — offer confirmatory CVS/amniocentesis, not a diagnosis
Low fetal fraction / “no result”→redraw or escalate to diagnostic testing
CVS / amniocentesis karyotype→definitive diagnosis of aneuploidy/genetic disorder
🧪Fetal RHD cfDNA
Targets anti-D to RhD-positive fetuses only
🧬NIPT
High-sensitivity screen for T21/T18/T13
🩸CVS
Diagnostic placental biopsy, 11–14 wks
💧Amniocentesis
Diagnostic amniotic fluid, ≥15 wks
4Pitfalls & limitations
Low fetal fraction (early gestation, high maternal BMI) can give an uninformative or falsely reassuring result.
NIPT false positives arise from confined placental mosaicism, vanishing twin or maternal copy-number/malignancy — a positive is never diagnostic.
CVS carries a small risk of placental mosaicism; amniocentesis before 15 weeks raises limb defect and loss risk, so timing matters.
🚩 NIPT is a SCREENING test: a “high chance” result must be confirmed by invasive diagnostic testing (CVS/amniocentesis) before any irreversible decision such as termination. Invasive tests themselves carry a procedure-related miscarriage risk of roughly 0.5–1%, so counselling and informed consent are essential.
🎓 One maternal blood tube of cell-free fetal DNA does double duty: it genotypes the fetal RHD gene to target anti-D prophylaxis AND screens for the common trisomies — but only invasive karyotyping is diagnostic.
